Satellite 813 Challenge · Track 2 Precision Agriculture · Proof of concept

AgriLens: Dust or Drought?

When a field's greenness drops, the cause could be dust, water shortage, harvest or simply a hazy satellite image. AgriLens flags unusual changes, checks the image quality and regional context, and tells the agronomist where to inspect before any irrigation decision is made.

How AgriLens works

From a satellite image to a field visit, in four steps

AgriLens does not name a cause. It finds unusual changes, checks whether the image itself can be trusted, and gives the agronomist a short list of places to look.

  2. STEP 01

    Detect change

    Compare each field's NDVI with the median of its previous three observations.

    615 observations checked, 36 outside ±0.110

  3. STEP 02

    Check the evidence

    Test image quality: aerosol load, unclassified pixels and long gaps between images.

    13 flags from the hazy 17 May scene set aside

  4. STEP 03

    Build a review list

    Rank the flags worth inspecting and set scene artefacts aside.

    23 review candidates: 14 positive (NDVI above expected) and 9 negative (below expected)

  5. STEP 04

    Inspect in the field

    The agronomist checks the crop, irrigation records and root-zone moisture.

    0 verified so far, so the cause stays undetermined

Reading the maps

What is NDVI?

Healthy leaves absorb most red light for photosynthesis and reflect much of the near-infrared light, which our eyes cannot see. Bare soil reflects both at similar levels. Satellites measure both, and NDVI compares them:

NDVI = (NIR − Red) ÷ (NIR + Red)

NDVI runs from −1 to +1. On these maps, values near 0 are bare soil and values close to 0.85 are dense, healthy crop.

A drop in NDVI means a field looks less green to the satellite. It does not say why. Dust, water shortage, harvest or a hazy image can all lower it, so AgriLens checks the image before anyone acts.

Image quality check

Why 17 May is set aside

Haze can make a whole scene look less green at once. Here is the same 3 × 3 km area on 5 May, 17 May and 20 May.

5 May
before
17 May
hazy scene
20 May
3 days later

The 17 May scene is visibly washed out and recovers within days. This is why its 13 flags are not counted as alerts.

Haze and greenness across all 33 field dates

17 May sceneOther dates

Suspected atmospheric scene effect (high aerosol load); not counted as an alert. On 17 May the aerosol thickness reached 0.85, the highest of all 33 dates. Mean NDVI across all 20 fields fell from 0.47 to 0.36 and recovered to 0.45 three days later. A dip across the whole region that reverses in three days fits a hazy image better than crop damage. This reading rests on pixel-quality data and the NDVI maps above; it has not been checked in the field.

Forecast benchmark

Persistence is the reference

Can a model predict a field's next NDVI better than assuming nothing changes? Not on the held-out fields.

Forecast error with 95% intervals

Persistence (reference)Other models

Next-observation NDVI forecast, scored as mean absolute error (lower is better) with 95% field-bootstrap intervals. Evaluated on 37 pairs from 5 held-out fields in one Nile Delta locality. Persistence is the reference. Ridge did better on the validation fields but not on the held-out test, so it is not presented as an improvement.

Show as a table
ModelValidation MAE (95% CI)Test MAE (95% CI)
Persistence (reference)0.0302 (0.0255–0.0349)0.0275 (0.0197–0.0374)
Median of last 30.0344 (0.0259–0.0458)0.0302 (0.0232–0.0417)
Ridge (exploratory)0.0215 (0.0165–0.0283)0.0355 (0.0292–0.0435)

How to read it

  • Persistence predicts that the next NDVI equals the latest one. It is the reference any model has to beat.
  • Each dot is the mean absolute error. The line through it is the 95% interval from resampling whole fields. Lower is better.
  • Ridge did better on the 6 validation fields. On the 5 held-out test fields its error is higher than persistence, and the difference is within the uncertainty.
  • With 5 test fields, the intervals are wide. The test covers the eastern strip of one locality in one season.

Honest limits

What the prototype can and cannot claim

What AgriLens shows today

  • Flags observations whose NDVI departs from the field's own recent history
  • Separates likely image problems (haze, unclassified pixels, long gaps) from flags worth inspecting
  • Shows each flag with regional dust, aerosol and soil-moisture context
  • Uses real Sentinel-2 and NASA EMIT data with geographic train/validation/test splits

What it cannot claim yet

  • That any flag was caused by dust or by drought
  • Any dust-versus-drought accuracy, yield, or water-saving figure
  • That the Ridge model beats persistence
  • That results hold beyond this 3 × 3 km locality and one season

Dust or Drought? — exploratory screening; independent field verification required.

Data: team-audited AgriLens database (615 field-date rows, SHA-256 5919ffbd…c30c6), validation package by Rama, modeling by Rand, data release by Maya. Dust, aerosol and soil-moisture values are regional model outputs that are the same for every field on a given date.

NDVI maps: 34 Sentinel-2 acquisitions on a 150 × 150 grid of 20 m pixels (UTM zone 36N), from the team's pixel table. 6 March has only 2.1% usable pixels, which is why the maps have 34 dates and the field table has 33.
